sentences.text: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market, also named the AI Labor Market Tracker, is an interactive tracker with regular updates whose evidence is an observed employment outcome and an exposure estimate (Labor Vector record); by its operator's account it "contains The Budget Lab's ongoing analysis of potential AI impacts on the labor market" (tracker PDF).

Its operator is The Budget Lab at Yale, its pages under Yale University's copyright (tracker page; Labor Vector record), Martha Gimbel the Lab's executive director (first report); the census places it at the distribution of gains and losses and asks of it "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" (Labor Vector record).

The analysis began as "Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs" by Gimbel, Molly Kinder of Brookings Metro, Joshua Kendall and Maddie Lee, dated 1 October 2025 (first report), a title the census carries as one of the tracker's names (Labor Vector record); it asked whether labor-market change in the 33 months since ChatGPT's release differed from past technological change and whether there were economy-wide employment effects, and it planned regular updates (first report).

The tracker was published on 16 July 2026 and updated to Version 1.0 on 15 September 2026, its data downloadable (tracker PDF), its page dated 14 October 2026 with the same plan of regular updates (tracker page); the census records it as active, founded on 16 July 2026, its data access 'Download All Data' and its licence unstated beyond Yale's copyright (Labor Vector record).

It refers its churn and the exposure of the unemployed to Gimbel et al. (2025) and its exposure metrics to Gimbel, Kendall and Kulsakdinun (2026) (tracker PDF), works the census lists as unread (Labor Vector record), and which match by authors and year the first report and the Lab's exposure review of 19 February 2026 (first report; exposure review).

It works in three sections, occupational churn, AI metrics, and comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers (tracker PDF), over monthly CPS microdata, its object the occupational mix, employment and unemployment as they relate to AI exposure and usage (Labor Vector record).

Churn is a dissimilarity index of the occupational mix adapted from Duncan and Duncan over monthly CPS data (first report); it "simply reflects change — it does not take a stance on the cause of that change" (first report), and it does not rely on exposure metrics while it "does not formally attempt to identify effects of AI" (Nunn's note).

The comparisons use synthetic differences-in-differences, which in Ryan Nunn's note of 7 May 2026 helps "to distinguish any genuine impact of AI on exposed occupations from the persistent differences between exposed and unexposed jobs" (Nunn's note); the census's method lists it with the churn, exposure and usage measures (Labor Vector record).

The tracker's takeaways are that the occupational mix "is not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI into the workforce", that measures of AI usage "show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment", and that the synthetic differences-in-differences analysis "does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint" (tracker page; Labor Vector record).

The September 2026 update, on August 2026 CPS microdata, "does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI", churn, the exposure of the unemployed and usage data remaining flat, within historical ranges or on pre-AI trends (tracker PDF; Labor Vector record).

In October 2025 the first report had found the occupational mix changing "more quickly than it has in the past", by no large difference and from before AI's widespread introduction, by industry a limited effect, across the broader labor market no discernible disruption in 33 months, and the anxiety over AI's effects "largely speculative" on its data (first report).

It found exposure, automation and augmentation measures unrelated to employment or unemployment, the shares of workers in low, middle and high exposure groups stable at about 29%, 46% and 18%, no clear growth in the exposure of the unemployed, and Anthropic's usage data stable "rather than disruption" (first report).

For recent college graduates the dissimilarity against older workers rose slightly faster, which "could be consistent with" Brynjolfsson et al. and "could also simply reflect a slowing labor market", the results to be read with caution for small samples (first report).

Nunn's note found the estimated effect on employment in the average exposed occupation, and on inflation-adjusted hourly wages, "close to zero" and statistically indistinguishable from it, the results not yet showing "clear indication of labor market effects of AI" (Nunn's note).

Around it the labor market had cooled, unemployment rising from 3.4% in April 2023 to 4.3% in March 2026 with low layoffs and low hiring, payroll growth held down in principal part by slower net immigration, and the conjecture that the cooling bears the imprint of employers' AI adoption is not supported by "the weight of the evidence—to date" (Nunn's note).

Its limit is in its wording: "Of course, these findings may change as new data become available" (tracker PDF; Labor Vector record); the first report "is not predictive of the future" and holds it "too soon to tell how disruptive the technology will be to jobs" (first report); the exposure review asks for humility about where AI disruption could go (exposure review); and Nunn's note expects AI "quite likely to eventually leave its mark on the labor market, even if it has not already" (Nunn's note).
The census keeps the finding from its opposite: the tracker is "NOT a finding that AI has no labor market effect: it states the analysis does not yet clearly indicate one" (Labor Vector record).

Its exposure measure in the first report is OpenAI's, whether ChatGPT-4 technology can cut an occupation's task time by at least 50%, "a theoretical estimate" not based on actual usage, and its usage measure Anthropic's data on one tool, Claude, comprehensive usage data being "not publicly available" (first report).

The exposure review places the Lab among the analysts who use Eloundou et al.'s exposure metrics and compares seven, Microsoft researchers' applicability score from Copilot conversations among them, finding broad agreement and more disagreement on highly exposed occupations, in magnitude more than in whether an occupation is exposed; exposure, it states, "is not indicative of a jobs AI will automate out of existence" but "indicates places in the labor market where AI could have an impact" (exposure review).

Claude usage alone, the first report states, "is not representative of how workers across the economy are using AI chatbots and tools", and better data, "comprehensive usage data from all the leading AI companies", is what it asks for (first report); the census records the tracker as "NOT a usage dataset: it uses usage measures as inputs" and lists which usage data it draws on, and their provider, as unread in its saved text (Labor Vector record).

On the census's reading the tracker's evidence can answer whether churn has left its historical ranges, whether AI-exposed workers are over-represented among the unemployed and whether usage tracks employment, and cannot answer "who supplies, directs or gains from labor performed with AI" or "effects below the level the CPS can detect"; it records supplier, director and gains as not recorded (Labor Vector record).

In the census's worked questions it is the observed tracker of "occupational churn and unemployment by exposure, from the CPS", one of two observed trackers whose readings of the same period differ, with "no clear labor-market footprint yet, at the level the CPS can see", and its meeting with Labor Vector's instruments is "none stated" (Labor Vector record).

The archive classes such measurement as AI-economics research that measures "which jobs AI eliminates, what tasks it can perform, and what consumer surplus it generates", Eloundou et al.'s capability projection among it (#716), whose exposure metrics the Lab uses (exposure review).

Beside it the archive defines a fourth channel, "compositional authority transfer", the rate at which AI synthesis captures value from authors by stripping attribution: "even when human labor *remains* (the author's work is used), the economic value tied to provenance — reputation, traffic, citation credit, contractual rights — is extracted by the system", which "is not displacement" (#716).

The census's question of who gains finds that "No record in the census measures the distribution of productivity gains between workers, employers, platforms and model providers" (Labor Vector record).

At 'Yale Budget Lab AI labor market' Google's AI Overview, on a baseline where no card cites the Labor Vector record, names the tracker, its conclusion, methods and sections from the Lab's own pages and holds the name, the data through September 2026, flat churn and the synthetic differences-in-differences design (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry records the 'yet' of "does not yet clearly indicate" dropped, wage trends, a 'Capital vs. Labor' line and a 'slight volatility' composed beyond the record, and the usage measures' providers left unsaid (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
It reads the composition as a provisional finding "composed as a settled negative", the 'yet' being "the whole of its claim" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Wikipedia has no article on the tracker or on the Lab; its article on generative AI cites the first report for "a 2025 study concluded that the US labor market had so far not experienced a discernible disruption from generative AI" (Wikipedia).
A Quest Means Business video carries the Lab's executive director "on why AI hasn't disrupted ..." (video card, title only).

The tracker was published on 16 July 2026 and updated to Version 1.0 on 15 September 2026, its data downloadable (tracker PDF), its page dated 14 October 2026 with the same plan of regular updates (tracker page); the census records it as active, founded on 16 July 2026, its data access 'Download All Data' and its licence unstated beyond Yale's copyright (Labor Vector record). It refers its churn and the exposure of the unemployed to Gimbel et al. (2025) and its exposure metrics to Gimbel, Kendall and Kulsakdinun (2026) (tracker PDF), works the census lists as unread (Labor Vector record), and which match by authors and year the first report and the Lab's exposure review of 19 February 2026 (first report; exposure review). It works in three sections, occupational churn, AI metrics, and comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers (tracker PDF), over monthly CPS microdata, its object the occupational mix, employment and unemployment as they relate to AI exposure and usage (Labor Vector record). Churn is a dissimilarity index of the occupational mix adapted from Duncan and Duncan over monthly CPS data (first report); it "simply reflects change — it does not take a stance on the cause of that change" (first report), and it does not rely on exposure metrics while it "does not formally attempt to identify effects of AI" (Nunn's note). The comparisons use synthetic differences-in-differences, which in Ryan Nunn's note of 7 May 2026 helps "to distinguish any genuine impact of AI on exposed occupations from the persistent differences between exposed and unexposed jobs" (Nunn's note); the census's method lists it with the churn, exposure and usage measures (Labor Vector record). The tracker's takeaways are that the occupational mix "is not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI into the workforce", that measures of AI usage "show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment", and that the synthetic differences-in-differences analysis "does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint" (tracker page; Labor Vector record). The September 2026 update, on August 2026 CPS microdata, "does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI", churn, the exposure of the unemployed and usage data remaining flat, within historical ranges or on pre-AI trends (tracker PDF; Labor Vector record). In October 2025 the first report had found the occupational mix changing "more quickly than it has in the past", by no large difference and from before AI's widespread introduction, by industry a limited effect, across the broader labor market no discernible disruption in 33 months, and the anxiety over AI's effects "largely speculative" on its data (first report). It found exposure, automation and augmentation measures unrelated to employment or unemployment, the shares of workers in low, middle and high exposure groups stable at about 29%, 46% and 18%, no clear growth in the exposure of the unemployed, and Anthropic's usage data stable "rather than disruption" (first report). For recent college graduates the dissimilarity against older workers rose slightly faster, which "could be consistent with" Brynjolfsson et al. and "could also simply reflect a slowing labor market", the results to be read with caution for small samples (first report). Nunn's note found the estimated effect on employment in the average exposed occupation, and on inflation-adjusted hourly wages, "close to zero" and statistically indistinguishable from it, the results not yet showing "clear indication of labor market effects of AI" (Nunn's note). Around it the labor market had cooled, unemployment rising from 3.4% in April 2023 to 4.3% in March 2026 with low layoffs and low hiring, payroll growth held down in principal part by slower net immigration, and the conjecture that the cooling bears the imprint of employers' AI adoption is not supported by "the weight of the evidence—to date" (Nunn's note). Its limit is in its wording: "Of course, these findings may change as new data become available" (tracker PDF; Labor Vector record); the first report "is not predictive of the future" and holds it "too soon to tell how disruptive the technology will be to jobs" (first report); the exposure review asks for humility about where AI disruption could go (exposure review); and Nunn's note expects AI "quite likely to eventually leave its mark on the labor market, even if it has not already" (Nunn's note). The census keeps the finding from its opposite: the tracker is "NOT a finding that AI has no labor market effect: it states the analysis does not yet clearly indicate one" (Labor Vector record). Its exposure measure in the first report is OpenAI's, whether ChatGPT-4 technology can cut an occupation's task time by at least 50%, "a theoretical estimate" not based on actual usage, and its usage measure Anthropic's data on one tool, Claude, comprehensive usage data being "not publicly available" (first report). The exposure review places the Lab among the analysts who use Eloundou et al.'s exposure metrics and compares seven, Microsoft researchers' applicability score from Copilot conversations among them, finding broad agreement and more disagreement on highly exposed occupations, in magnitude more than in whether an occupation is exposed; exposure, it states, "is not indicative of a jobs AI will automate out of existence" but "indicates places in the labor market where AI could have an impact" (exposure review). Claude usage alone, the first report states, "is not representative of how workers across the economy are using AI chatbots and tools", and better data, "comprehensive usage data from all the leading AI companies", is what it asks for (first report); the census records the tracker as "NOT a usage dataset: it uses usage measures as inputs" and lists which usage data it draws on, and their provider, as unread in its saved text (Labor Vector record). On the census's reading the tracker's evidence can answer whether churn has left its historical ranges, whether AI-exposed workers are over-represented among the unemployed and whether usage tracks employment, and cannot answer "who supplies, directs or gains from labor performed with AI" or "effects below the level the CPS can detect"; it records supplier, director and gains as not recorded (Labor Vector record). In the census's worked questions it is the observed tracker of "occupational churn and unemployment by exposure, from the CPS", one of two observed trackers whose readings of the same period differ, with "no clear labor-market footprint yet, at the level the CPS can see", and its meeting with Labor Vector's instruments is "none stated" (Labor Vector record). The archive classes such measurement as AI-economics research that measures "which jobs AI eliminates, what tasks it can perform, and what consumer surplus it generates", Eloundou et al.'s capability projection among it (#716), whose exposure metrics the Lab uses (exposure review). Beside it the archive defines a fourth channel, "compositional authority transfer", the rate at which AI synthesis captures value from authors by stripping attribution: "even when human labor *remains* (the author's work is used), the economic value tied to provenance — reputation, traffic, citation credit, contractual rights — is extracted by the system", which "is not displacement" (#716). The census's question of who gains finds that "No record in the census measures the distribution of productivity gains between workers, employers, platforms and model providers" (Labor Vector record). At 'Yale Budget Lab AI labor market' Google's AI Overview, on a baseline where no card cites the Labor Vector record, names the tracker, its conclusion, methods and sections from the Lab's own pages and holds the name, the data through September 2026, flat churn and the synthetic differences-in-differences design (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry records the 'yet' of "does not yet clearly indicate" dropped, wage trends, a 'Capital vs. Labor' line and a 'slight volatility' composed beyond the record, and the usage measures' providers left unsaid (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It reads the composition as a provisional finding "composed as a settled negative", the 'yet' being "the whole of its claim" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). Wikipedia has no article on the tracker or on the Lab; its article on generative AI cites the first report for "a 2025 study concluded that the US labor market had so far not experienced a discernible disruption from generative AI" (Wikipedia). A Quest Means Business video carries the Lab's executive director "on why AI hasn't disrupted ..." (video card, title only).

case.statement: The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The Labor Vector census record describes the tracker from the Lab's own pages, each field with its basis ('operator'), and answers for it the census's question (who supplies, directs and gains, and what kind of evidence the resource brings), recording its evidence as an observed employment outcome and an exposure estimate and stating what that evidence can and cannot settle; its negative tags keep the tracker's 'not yet' from a finding of no effect (LV-24) and the tracker from a usage dataset (LV-25). The capture record checks the composition against those pages (CAP-1-01, CAP-1-02). No deposit names the tracker or the Lab. One deposit bears on its class: #716 states what AI-economics research measures (labor displacement, capability projection: 'which jobs AI eliminates, what tasks it can perform') and adds, on that object, a channel it does not register, value extracted where labor remains ('This is not displacement; it is extraction without attribution'), as 'a fourth' beside the three it names. That is an addition of a sense and a limit to the field's own object, not a contest of its ontology; no defining paper supplies an ontology the field lacks: ρ = extends, the equal-terms case (§0.9, §1.2a). Labor Vector's own reading of where the tracker meets its instruments is 'none stated' (LV-19).

Existing AI-economics research addresses three channels: labor displacement, capability projection, and welfare estimation. PER addresses a fourth
NOT a finding that AI has no labor market effect: it states the analysis does not yet clearly indicate one

lv_intersection (where it meets DSL, task-origin and user labor drag: the archive's reading, kept apart from the resource's own terms)

E_F.definition: The Budget Lab at Yale's interactive tool 'Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market' (the AI Labor Market Tracker), published 16 July 2026, Version 1.0 of 15 September 2026, page of 14 October 2026, holding the Lab's 'ongoing analysis of potential AI impacts on the labor market' in three sections (occupational churn, AI metrics, comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers) on monthly CPS microdata; continuing the report of 1 October 2025 by Gimbel, Kinder, Kendall and Lee; its exposure inputs OpenAI's (Eloundou et al.) and six other metrics, its usage input Anthropic's Claude data; its finding that AI's labor-market footprint is not yet clear, with the stated limit that the findings may change.

E_A.definition: the same tracker, in the Labor Vector census record and the archive's deposits: an interactive tool whose evidence is an observed employment outcome and an exposure estimate, at the intersection of gains and losses, recording no supplier, director or recipient of gains; its finding 'NOT a finding that AI has no labor market effect'; its usage measures inputs from providers its saved text does not name; able to settle churn, exposure among the unemployed and usage against employment, and unable to settle who supplies, directs or gains; a member of the AI-economics research #716 describes as measuring which jobs AI eliminates and what tasks it can perform, beside which #716 sets a fourth channel, value extracted where labor remains.

translation.received: F11 (B1, ¶3): "First, is the pace of labor market change in this 33-month period of employment disruption different from past periods of early technological change?
